utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. And good afternoon, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Defence, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Ms. Nikolic. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Very shortly you will be starting your testimony as a Defence witness for the accused, General Miletic. Before you do so, you are required under our rules to enter a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Text is right in front of you, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Fauveau will put some questions to you. She will then be followed by others on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, this is a witness who wants the 92 ter to be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you know what the procedure is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you tell us what are your name and Christian name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: My name is Ivan Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember making a declaration about General Miletic in July [as interpreted] last year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you been able to look at this statement in the last few days?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is page 2, line 13. It is the month of May, correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, for that, Madam Fauveau. And it will be taken care of. At page 2, line 13, instead of "July" we put "May." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this statement reflect what you told?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave this statement to the best of my recollection and it does correspond with my memory of the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions today, would you say exactly the same thing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have any new information that I might add.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to read a summary of the declaration made by the witness, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The witness was a professional officer in the JNA, and later in the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then in the army of Serbia-Montenegro. He was a lieutenant general when he retired. He met General Miletic when General Miletic was a student at the national defence school in Belgrade in the early 1990s. At the time, the witness worked at the Technical Military Institute in Belgrade. During these professional encounters, they got to know each other better and became personal friends and close personal friends. They remained friends since then until today, and the witness describes their friendship as a sincere and lasting friendship. Since the beginning of their friendship and until General Miletic left for The Hague, they would meet regularly and spend time together on important occasions in their respective families, such as promotions or weddings. The witness remembers that with his wife, he attended a lunch which took place in the Miletic family's apartment in order to celebrate Maja's 18th birthday, Maja being General Miletic's daughter. Her birthday is the 10th of July and was celebrated one or two days before that date. A few days before the lunch, Radivoje Miletic invited her, with his wife [as interpreted], to attend this lunch at his flat in Novi Belgrade. General Miletic, his wife Vica, and their son, Zoran, were present during this lunch which took place on the Saturday or on the Sunday, and during which about a dozen people were present. Zoran Matejic was one of the guests. The witness remembers Zoran Matejic because they worked together at the technical institute, and they haven't seen each other since then. The witness also remembers an older general called Banjac. He doesn't remember anyone else being present. General Miletic, that's the majority -- that his daughter Maja's coming years was the main reason for that celebration, but General Miletic's promotion to the grade of general was also celebrated. The witness is a friend of General Miletic and has a very high opinion of him. He considers him as an extremely professional officer and thinks that he has all the qualities of a good and honest person. End of quote of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the 5D92 to be put into the file. It is the witness statement on the 28th of May, 2008. And I would like to inform the Chamber that there is a slight mistake in paragraph 6, 5D1392. Paragraph 6, in the English version you can read - page 2 of the English version - [In English] Chief of the administration for cooperation and planning. [Interpretation] And the witness indeed said in B/C/S the head of the administration of operations and education.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, may I ask you a number of questions. First of all, could you describe your professional background, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I graduated from the airforce technical academy, then higher airforce academy, and I worked for over 20 years in the military technical institute. After that, I worked as the chief of the airforce technical administration. All of the equipment of the airforce was within our purview. After that I was the assistant Minister for Defence of materiel, and I was assistant commander for the Main Staff for logistics. As far as my extra-military activities are concerned, I taught at the electrical engineering faculty in Belgrade, and now I am a professor at the university in Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your statement you mentioned that you knew that General Miletic's daughter's birthday was on the 10th of July. Could you perhaps explain how you knew that her birthday was on the 18th -- on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to admit that not many dates stick in my memory, including dates from my military career that are important for me, but this date did stick in my memory because this happened immediately before the fall of Srebrenica and the media campaign exploitation of the event, which was really quite intense. As a soldier, I knew that Srebrenica was a protected area, and it came as a surprise to me. And it fixed my attention. So these two events, their correlation, stuck in my mind. And this is how I was able to determine that it did, indeed, happen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just one more question. What was your grade in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In 1995 I was a colonel, and I promoted to general in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Any of the Defence teams would like to put questions or cross-examination to the witness? I see none. I hear none. Mr. Vanderpuye, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon. Good afternoon to you, and Your Honours, good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, General Djokic. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye, and on behalf of the Prosecution I will put some questions to you in relation to your direct examination that was conducted by my colleague. Now, in relation to your direct examination, you referred to a statement that you gave in May of 2008, and I believe it's on the 29th of May, 2008. And you recall giving that statement and signing it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to giving the statement, I take it you had an opportunity to speak with Defence Counsel for General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on the 29th of May, which is the date of the statement, was that the first time that you had met with the Defence Counsel or anyone from the Defence of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No, maybe two or three months before that, Mr. Petrusic, General Miletic's Defence Counsel, asked me if I recalled this event. Of course, I couldn't recall it right there on the spot and I had to consult my wife to put this whole picture together because a long time had elapsed. And once I got together the picture that I presented in the statement, I got in touch with him and I told him that I remembered the event and that I put the things that I remembered into the statement. And then, after a while, let's say maybe two months, I went to Mr. Petrusic's office and we drafted this statement and I signed it. That's the statement that you have in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see, okay. In relation to the -- the first meeting that you had with the Miletic Defence, that would have been that meeting that you had with Mr. Petrusic, I think you said, yes, two or three months before you actually signed the statement; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you hadn't been contacted by anyone from the Defence prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: This was the first contact, both regarding this issue and, indeed, in general, the first time that this case was discussed and my knowledge, if any, of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So we are talking about March, May of 2000 -- well, I'm sorry, March and February of 2008 was your first contact with the Miletic Defence as concerns the events that are in your statement in July of 1995, that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please repeat. We didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the interpreters didn't catch his answer. If you could elicit it again from him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your answer, I don't think the interpreters were able to hear you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, the first contact regarding my statement and my memory of the events about this lunch, celebratory lunch was March 2008, but I don't recall the exact date when I gave statement but I think it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you contacted by anybody besides the Defence in relation to the celebratory events that were recorded in your statement before you met Mr. Petrusic at any point?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any such contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you weren't contacted by General Miletic's wife or son or daughter in relation to these events in July 1995 back before March of 2008?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't discuss those issues with them. Even after I gave my statement we didn't have any contacts regarding this statement, and this is all I can say regarding our contacts in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you been in contact with General Miletic since he was transferred to The Hague in relation to these charges?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I think we met twice when he came to Belgrade, once I think he had a death in the family and I saw him for maybe ten minutes in this regard, and the second time was when I went with my son and some of his friends after a basketball game. We all went to the basketball game, and when the game was over we went over to see him. So these are two contacts that I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you remember about when those were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact time. One of those meetings when I came over with the children may have been in, let's say, 2006, but I can't really recall. I didn't know that you would be asking me this question. I -- otherwise I would have checked when the game was, because I was not there alone. There were several of us. And the second event was when General Miletic's sister died, if I am not mistaken. That was the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember when about that was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So your recollection is to the celebratory events that are recorded in your statement, that is, to specifically when they are occurred, is based upon your conversations with your wife. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I recall that event, both on the basis of that conversation, but I also told you about this correlation between that event and the events that followed the situation in the media, the way it was painted, the fall of Srebrenica. So these are the two elements that led me to remember this event and made me remember that it all happened around the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you obviously know General Miletic's family, you know his wife, you know his daughter and his son. Would you consider yourself a relatively close family friend?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I think we are close friends, and I can only wish that General Miletic saw it in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you have some reason to think he doesn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a question, if I understand well, it's a question of interpretation. Let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that General Miletic was transferred to The Hague or came to The Hague in relation to these charges of this case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know the -- do you know the year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I suppose it was maybe three or four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Three or four years ago?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that's about as best as you can do. Can you tell us what month?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no, I can't remember. We didn't discuss it, so -- I didn't discuss it with my family, either. I really feel uncomfortable discussing matters that might be unpleasant for the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, you indicated in your statement that you were surprised to learn that Srebrenica had fallen. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that now in my oral response.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreters are having difficulties following what you are saying. If you could come nearer to the microphones, that would help a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You were surprised to hear that Srebrenica had fallen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Well, you know that I was a soldier. I also knew that Srebrenica was protected by the United Nations, and when that happened, when this was made public, the only logical explanation for me was that in the chaos of war that there was some kind of an agreement between the warring factions and the international community. I did not have any other explanation, any other things that could have triggered that, because the international community was deeply involved and was present throughout the time involved in all the events. And, after all, Srebrenica was declared a protected area by the international community, so nothing else seemed logical to me. Any change in the status of that area came as a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did you discuss that at all with your friend, General Miletic, at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: We did not have an opportunity to discuss this because if we are talking about this feast, this lunch, no topics related to his job, to the developments in Republika Srpska, were discussed. And later on, when it was made public that Srebrenica had fallen, General Miletic was not in Belgrade anymore and we did not discuss it. After the fall of Srebrenica, we know that there were all kinds of contradictory points of view presented in the media. There was this media campaign about the interpretation of the events, and this took a different shape. But my explanation was as I just told you. An area protected by the international community could only change its status with the knowledge of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Do you know, or can you recall, I should say, when it was that you learned that General Miletic was in town in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Well, the birthday was celebrated over the weekend. I don't know whether it was the 9th or the 10th. I really can't tell you whether it was the 9th or the 10th, but it was over the weekend. And then two or three days before that, let's say, General Miletic invited us to this lunch. So I suppose that he had come to Belgrade before that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say "invited," he invited you over the telephone or he invited you in person?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And he didn't indicate to you at the time of that telephone call where he was calling from, did he?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that he left Belgrade after you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know when he left Belgrade. All I know is that at this lunch, since there were many people there, we did not have an opportunity to sit down together and have a chat. And there was a deal that after this lunch was over, we would go somewhere and have a drink and talk. After that, he didn't get in touch with me. We didn't speak again, after that, and I suppose that after the news came about the fall of Srebrenica that he went back to his post. But that's my assumption. I did not talk to him so I don't have the exact information about when he actually went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I would like to show you one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for this, Mr. President, I would greatly appreciate it. It's a 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure, let's go into it private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Mr. Vanderpuye has just concluded his cross-examination. Is there redirect, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon, Judge Stole, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokic, we have come to the end of your testimony. We have no further questions for you, which means you are free to go. You will receive all the assistance that you require. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I thank you for having come over to give testimony and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, I don't suppose you have any documents except for the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the statement 5D [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Which I don't suppose is objected to because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it's at the heart of the 92 ter procedure. Thank you. Do you have any documents to tender --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The intercept is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16, line 22. 5D1392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, I was going to ask you that precisely. So that concludes the testimony of Mr. Djokic. Next witness. You wish to make any statements before the witness is admitted into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No warning or anything of the sort? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The statement of the witness contains a mistake in paragraph 6. Some lines have been omitted in the translation in English. We have requested a corrected translation, and we are sure that it will arrive perhaps today or at the latest, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, Mr. Matejic, you are required under our rules to make a solemn declaration that you will be speaking the truth. That's the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. You are going to be asked some questions by Madam Fauveau for General Miletic. She will then be followed on cross-examination by others. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please let us now your name and first name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Matejic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember making a statement for the Defence of General Miletic in May 2008?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity on review this statement recently?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this statement reflect accurately --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you were asked questions today, would you make the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to read the summary of the statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The witness has met General Miletic in 1967 in Zadar where he was at the military academy in the anti-aircraft defence. The witness, and Radivoje Miletic, remained friends and because of this strong friendship, they became particularly close. This sort of friendship is traditional for Serbs and is considered as a family tie. General Miletic continued to serve at Zadar after he had finished the military academy. The two remained in contact by correspondence after the witness had left Zadar and came to Belgrade. They used to meet three or four times a year. Radivoje Miletic was in Zadar until the beginning of the 1990s. The witness believes Radivoje Miletic came to the school of national defence in Belgrade in the fall of 1990. The witness knows that Radivoje Miletic was in the army of the Republika Srpska from 1992 until the end of the war and for a certain period after the signing of the Dayton Agreements. The witness confirms that Radivoje Miletic came to Belgrade in July 1995, a few days before the 10th of July 1995. He knows that the birthday of General Miletic's daughter, Maja, is on the 10th of July, and that in 1995 she was becoming of age. This day is particularly celebrated since all other birthdays -- more than other birthdays, and it was also the case in the Miletic family. The witness is sure that Radivoje Miletic called him and told him that they had two reasons to have a celebration feast. The witness asked him what was the second reason, since he knew that the first reason was the 18th birthday of Maja. Radivoje Miletic told him that he had recently promoted to the rank of general. Radivoje Miletic invited him with his wife to the lunch which was prepared by the Miletic family on this occasion. This lunch took place two or three days after Radivoje Miletic made that call. It was not a weekday. It was a Saturday or a Sunday. The witness and his wife accepted the invitation and went to this lunch. Radivoje Miletic, his wife, Vica, and their children were present as well as the invited people; among which Colonel Petar Djuric and his wife, and their common friend, General -- retired General Nenad Banjac, retired, who is ever since deceased, and Ivan Djokic and his wife. The witness knows Ivan Djokic because they worked together in the technical institute. They stayed in the apartment of the Miletic family until late. And Radivoje Miletic told him that he was going to stay in Belgrade three or four days before returning to Republika Srpska. They agreed that during the stay of Radivoje Miletic in Belgrade, he and his wife would come at the witness' place. One or two days after this luncheon, Radivoje Miletic called the witness and told him about the fall of Srebrenica, which was a surprise for him, too. Radivoje Miletic told him that they couldn't see each other because he was going to return to Republika Srpska. This conversation took place before the evening news, because the witness heard on the news that the army of the Republika Srpska had entered Srebrenica. This news surprised him, even though Radivoje Miletic had told him, because the information broadcast the proceeding days did not let people think that Srebrenica was going to be taken. The family of the witness and the family of General Miletic are very close. Radivoje Miletic has all the qualities of an exceptionally honest and worthy person, dignified person. He is full of respect and consideration for his friends and respects differences. He was never intolerant towards members of other nations or religions. He has lived for a long time in Croatia, his wife is Croatian, and he has got friends of several nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would request this, 5D1393, to be admitted. This is a statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I hear none for the other Defence teams, so it's so admitted. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam. [In English] I would be surprised if there are questions for the other Defence teams, none, in fact. Mr. Vanderpuye, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye, and on behalf of the Prosecution I will --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- I will put some questions to you in relation to your statement. Now, as I understand it you gave a statement to the -- to the Defence of General Miletic on the 30th of May, 2008. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, and it appears that you gave an interview to General Miletic's Defence attorney, Mr. Petrusic. Is that right as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And prior to giving that statement on the 30th of May, 2008, had you met with the Defence of General Miletic or anybody representing that Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: In 2007, in the second half of that year, I met Counsel Petrusic, and he asked me whether I wished to make a statement concerning this matter. I agreed, and that was all we said during that conversation. We didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- in the second half of 2007, you mean, I guess, sometime between -- well, sometime after June of that year, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you can't be more specific than that, that's fair to say, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. He only asked me whether I could make a statement concerning that birthday party. I told him I could and that was the end of our conversation, except that we agreed that we would talk again at a later date, which we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first I just want to get clear that you can't be more specific in terms of a date of this conversation you had with Mr. Petrusic than it was in the second half of 2007. You can't be more specific than that, month, season?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: It was certainly in the summer. That's all I can say. Our conversation was brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who brought up the issue of the -- well, let me, before I ask you this question, let me ask you: Did you speak to anybody from the Defence prior to that, prior to this summertime conversation with Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you speak to anybody close to General Miletic prior to that, such as, well, General Miletic, his wife, his son, his daughter about this specific party, just so we are clear, before you met Mr. Petrusic in the summer of 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. When you met with Mr. Petrusic in the summer of 2007, as you indicated, the conversation was very brief, but who brought up the question of this party at that conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Counsel Petrusic called me, I came to his office, the conversation was not longer than 5 minutes. We agreed to talk later. It was only a preliminary conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, but who brought that up? Did he ask you, for example, Can you tell me a little bit about what you remember of July 1995. Or did he say something more directed, such as, There was a party in July 1995, can you tell me about whether you were there or what you know about it. Can you tell us who brought up this whole idea, this topic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: He asked me the following: Do you remember Maja's 18th birthday party. I told him I did. He said, if it becomes necessary for you to make a statement or to testify, do you agree. And I agreed in principle. And that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So at that time there were no details concerning the party discussed at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So at that time you never mentioned the date of the party to Mr. Petrusic or the time or the other guests, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The next time you met with Mr. Petrusic was when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: I think it was the second half of March, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Before I get to that meeting, let me just ask one other question about the one in 2007 in the summer. That lasted 5 minutes, you said. Now, when Mr. Petrusic asked you about whether you were at the party, you were able to remember immediately that you were there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you hadn't spoken to anybody about that party, well, in how long?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Except with my family, ever since that party took place until the time I talked about it to Mr. Petrusic, I didn't speak about the party with anyone except my family members of my recollections of that day and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And how long ago was that -- how long was that before you met Mr. Petrusic? When was the last time you spoke about this party with your family members before you met Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember what the occasion was that you spoke about it a year before you met Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really recall that. But, at any rate, that event was mentioned in various cases; for instance, when my children's birthdays came up. But at any rate, we would talk about this birthday on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You met with Mr. Petrusic in the second half of March of 2008. That's true, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you remember the specific date that you met with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you meet with him in his office or someplace else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And on that occasion did you speak to him for more than five minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it on that occasion that you discussed with him some of the details concerning what is recounted in your statement concerning the events of July 1995, the party in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Only about this feast and perhaps some inconsequential talk about this topic but that conversation may have lasted half an hour, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. On that particular date, you didn't give him a statement, right? You didn't sign any statement or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have it clear, because "no, no, yes, yes," in a few months' time, might confuse us. So what's your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second half of March, I came to Mr. Petrusic for a preliminary discussion about the statement that I was to provide. I don't know whether this suffices by way of an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't sign any statement on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you spoke with Mr. Petrusic on that occasion, I take it you provided him with some details concerning this party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Listed in my statement, described in my statement, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And at that time he wrote down what you told him, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't recall. It's possible that he did make some notes, but I am not sure. I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But was he the only person there at the time that you had this meeting or were there other people there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: We were alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the next time you met with him, was that on the 30th of May, 2008?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you give him a separate -- well, did you go over the same party again with him on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk. We started drafting the statement. If you consider that a discussion or a conversation, then we did. We actually talked and then Mr. Petrusic started taking down the statement. I, in other words, started giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, sir, between the time -- well, you consider yourself a close friend of General Miletic, obviously, very close family friend, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you, of course, remember when it was that he was transferred to The Hague in relation to the charges in this case, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when was that, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, on the 28th of February, and I forgot the year. But I remember the date, the 28th of February, and I don't think that the year is at issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, between the time that he was transferred to The Hague in 2005 and 2007, that you met with Mr. Petrusic, and even today, have you spoken to General Miletic about this particular party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the other microphone for the witness please be switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the usher please help him. We need your other -- well, they are both switched on, from -- at least what I can see. Yes. No, no, no, don't bother about it. Let's proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you spoken to him about anything in relation to this case since then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: You mean since his arrival in The Hague? Well, of course, we've spoken. The first thing we discussed was his health, then the length of the trial, the length of the Defence case, nothing more than that. Because I, as his good friend, am first and foremost interested in his health. That's my concern. And every time we saw each other, I would always ask him that first. And in the past, as far as his professional life is concerned, we never discussed it. Our professions are different, and to tell you the truth, I was not really interested in the military segment of his life --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you were --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: -- in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you as his good friend, I am sure, and I credit that you are interested in his health, but I would imagine that you would also be interested to know what he's charged with. And you might even be interested to know whether or not there is a case against him and what the case is about. That's fair to say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say that this interest that I had for his case focussed on making sure that he could be as stable and as healthy as possible in order to bear this whole thing. As for the information about the trial, the Prosecution case, the Defence case, well, that wouldn't mean anything to me. The only thing that matters for me is that this friend of mine, this year-long friend of mine, is able to get out of all this as an honest man and primarily as a man in good health.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATEJIC
utterances.text: All the other -- just a moment. I didn't evince any interest in his service, in what he was doing, I simply was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Any redirect, Ms. Fauveau, do you want to consult with your client?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We don't have any further questions for you, which means that brings to an end your testimony. I wish to thank you so much for having come over and I also wish you safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The statement has already been tendered, Ms. Fauveau. Any further documents? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there aren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That -- yes, the witness may leave. That concludes the testimony of this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next one we'll start after the break. I think we can take the break now. One thing I need to clear with you, Madam Fauveau, because I had some conflicting information. How much do you estimate your examination-in-chief to last with the next one, I mean? Five hours? That's the latest occasion that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says seven hours, but I don't think it will last seven hours. However, we have a problem with the following witness, because the Dutch authorities rejected his request for visa. So it's a bit tricky for us to plan things ahead, because it's going to last quite long with this witness. It's also the Pandurevic's team and Popovic team's witness, so it should last about -- about until Tuesday. However, I am not sure that with it -- at this time of year -- even Wednesday, possibly, but given the time of year I am not sure we will be able to find another witness to replace him, to replace the one that was supposed to come later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see when there is -- you don't have a problem with the visa for this next witness, he's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one is already here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So which one are you referring to, because you had a list until Friday. We did get a hint in the course of earlier on this week or last week that you may encounter a problem with the last one. That's 5DW4. Is that the one that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honour. At first we thought he wouldn't be prepared to come because the 19th of December is a family celebration in Serbia, but he was prepared to come. We made all arrangements, and yesterday the VWS section informed us that the Dutch authorities rejected his request for the visa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Jevdjevic, anyway, is going to be here with us for quite some time, because as you said, he is a common witness with others as well. So let's have the break now, and then we start.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned as a Defence witness by several of the Defence teams, and you are about to start giving evidence. I think I better tell you straight away that we won't finish with your testimony this week, so you will need to stay here the weekend, and then we will continue next week and hopefully by Tuesday or Wednesday we should finish with your testimony. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require from you that you enter or you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be speaking the truth, text of which has just been handed to you. Please read it out aloud and that almost your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Petrusic, from the Miletic Defence team, will be firing questions for seven hours or maybe a little bit less, and then we will see what happens afterwards. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, good afternoon to you, Your Honours. I hope that the time estimate for this witness will prove to be wrong, rather, that we will take shorter time than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jevdjevic, and first of all let me introduce myself. My name is Nenad Petrusic, and I will be asking you some questions on behalf of General Miletic's Defence this afternoon and again tomorrow. Right at the beginning, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the two of us speak the same language, and it is therefore necessary for you to wait for a short while before starting with your answer after I have asked you a question, in order for all this to be interpreted. Perhaps the best guidance would be to look at the cursor on the screen in front of you. Now, I would like you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us what schools did you complete?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the military secondary school in Belgrade, and then the military academy of the ground forces in Belgrade, signals department; and also the General Staff's school in the centre of high military schools in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, when did you start your service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Yugoslav Peoples' Army in 1986 when I graduated from the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what rank you held when you joined the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When I joined the JNA, I had the rank of the second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us something about your military career up until the time when the armed conflict broke out in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My first post was in the Uzice garrison where I was the commander of the signals platoon, and then in the same garrison, I also served as the company commander. Again, it was a signals company. And those were the posts that I held until the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And where were you when the war in the former Yugoslavia broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia, I was in Uzice, in my garrison. And in 1991, as a commander of a unit, I was sent to a front line in what is today the Republic of Croatia, I was deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was still the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was still the area, the territory of the former SFRY, and I served there as part of a unit of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, may I please remind you of what Mr. Petrusic told you in the beginning, to allow for a short pause before you answer the questions; otherwise, you will be causing problems for the interpreters. Thank you. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, at one point did you actually join the army of Republika Srpska and, if so, could you please tell us when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I joined the army of Republika Srpska in May 1992. And the first post that I held for about a month was in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. And then in June 1992 I was appointed to a post in the 65th Signals Regiment in the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka, near Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said it was the 65th Signals Regiment of the Main Staff. Did you perhaps make a mistake there as regards the numerical designation of the regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. It may have been the 67th Signals Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long did you serve in the 67th Signals Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in the 67th Signals Regiment until the 1st of November, 1992, until the time when the Drina Corps was established. This was when I was appointed the commander of the signals battalion in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, this is usual procedure when it comes to personal details of the witnesses, and I think that I omitted to do that. I actually forgot to ask you that. Could you please tell me when you were born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Rogatica, on the 11th of December, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So this was a little factual digression from your description of your military career. Now, I would like to ask you this: The Drina Corps, you mentioned the 1st of November as the date it was established. Could you please tell us where was it headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The first headquarters of the Drina Corps was in the Gora hotel in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what military post code that was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was military post code 7111, Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether between 1992 and 1995 there were any changes to the military post code of the Drina Corps? When I say "changes" I am talking about the numerical designation 7111.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: A couple of weeks after the Drina Corps was established with its headquarters in Han Pijesak, for operational and other reasons, the command was moved to Vlasenica. But I know that the designation for the military post code remained the same, 7111, Han Pijesak, in the period that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How long did you serve as the commander of the signals battalion in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I served there until the end of the war as the commander of the signals battalion in the Drina Corps, until the peace agreements were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After the war, what post did you hold in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After the war ended, I was first the commander of an infantry brigade in Sekovici, then the commander -- or, rather, the chief of signals in the 5th corps of the army of Republika Srpska, which was established in 1997, the headquarters was in Sokolac. And then I became the commander of an infantry brigade in the same corps in Visegrad. And I ended my military career as the assistant commander of the corps for morale, information, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what year did your military career end?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My career, as a professional in the military, ended in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us, finally, what is your occupation now, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I work in the Telekom of the Republika Srpska. I am an engineer in the mobile networks directorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you told us that you were in the Drina Corps, that you were the signals battalion commander. Are you aware that during the war, at some point in time, protected areas were established on the territory of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that in the course of the war in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, at a certain point in time, three protected areas were established; specifically, Srebrenica, Zepa, and a little later, Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware how it came about that the Srebrenica protected area was established?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1993, the Drina Corps was engaged in offensive activities on the area of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Kasaba, and from the south towards Srebrenica, Osmaci, Zeleni Jadar, and Pribicevac. And I recall that at one point in time, the order arrived that the Drina Corps and the other units of the army of Republika Srpska participating in that operation should interrupt the operation because there were negotiations going on between the two warring parties, their military and civilian authorities. And I remember that at that time UN forces entered Srebrenica headed by General Morillon, and I assume that it was around that time that Srebrenica was granted the status of a protected area. I participated personally in that operation which was stopped by our superior command for the reasons I have just stated. I was engaged in communications for the need of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that these areas were supposed to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that the first information concerning the demilitarisation of Srebrenica was forwarded to us, who were deployed there, in Pribicevac in 1993, came from General Zivanovic, the corps commander, personally. He told us this from his command post in Vlasenica, and he said that we should congratulate the officers and the unit commanders on their success up to that point in time. And he informed us that the entire area of Srebrenica was to be fully demilitarised. He said that the members of the 28th Division would hand over all their weapons to the UN forces, which were due to enter Srebrenica, and that there would no longer be any organised armed units in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1994 and 1995, were you an active participant in many combat activities conducted around the enclaves and launched from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the period you mentioned, I was personally engaged, more than once, in planning combat activities conducted by the Drina Corps or some of its units, in order to deal with the combat situation in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 5D1224 on the screen, please. The relevant part in the English version, the one we are interested in, is on page 2, point 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, please take a look this document, a look at this order, and look at item 1. Tell us whether you were aware of this situation regarding the behaviour of the Muslim forces in Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that throughout that period of time, from the time the peace agreement was signed, or, rather, from the time the safe areas of Srebrenica and Zepa were established, the Drina Corps was facing constant problems because of the military activities launched from those two enclaves. They could be described in different ways. One of the ways in which they took place was the infiltration of larger or smaller groups from the enclaves -- from one enclave to another, and vice versa, and from both enclaves towards Tuzla and towards Olovo and Kladanj, those general areas. I participated in the events at the time, and I was aware of all these activities. This is one of the documents showing this. It mentions these armed groups going towards Zvornik and Pale, and this was the only road dividing the Drina Corps in two halves, and these armed groups from those enclaves often crossed that road going towards Kladanj, Olovo, and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This road, the Zvornik-Pale road that is, was it in the depth of the territory of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was like a line dividing -- or, rather, like a line halfway between the these two enclaves and the other part of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; the corps, that is, and it's more or less 15 to 30 kilometres away from these enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have document 5D1032 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, the first passage is the relevant one, after the title, where it says, "Raising combat readiness to the highest level..." Please take a look at this paragraph. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the military authorities in Srebrenica and Zepa had, as their aim, the joining up of these two enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the Drina Corps, probably sent to all the units; although, it isn't expressly stated here, but I assume that the document was sent to all the units of the Drina Corps. And I personally am familiar with the situation. At the time, the corps command and all the units learned from intelligence and other sources that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was probably aiming at joining up these two enclaves with the largest part of their territory and that in certain periods of time, they would attempt to achieve this by military activity from both of those enclaves and in the other direction as well. And this is a document showing all this, this document mentions all this. And that's why the order was issued to all units to raise combat readiness to the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document, you can see that it really was sent to all the units in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what it says here. I was surprised not to see it in the heading, in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1038 on the screen. Excuse me, excuse me, before that, 5D1037.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, please look at paragraph 8 on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the English version it's also paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether at this time the forces of the Drina Corps undertook activities to prevent these incursions by armed groups from Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what this document shows. That's something that is the worst thing possible for a soldier when he feels that his back is not protected and that there is the possibility of sabotage groups infiltrating you, the depth of your territory, and wreaking havoc. From the information the corps received in that period of time, it was evident that this was a real threat. So certain measures were taken and the units were ordered to be active in preventing such enemy activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 5D1038 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at paragraph 1, the third paragraph in point 1, which begins with the words "Last night ..." Please read this passage.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had a problem with the microphone and there is an objection. Yes, one moment, Mr. Petrusic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These questions are more time consuming than they are probative, which I think is an important issue. This is 1994. These are not contested issues. Mr. Butler testified about this. I think the adjudicated facts have talked about this. This is an area that has been gone over and over again. I can direct the attention to a Muslim document from 1995 that -- from the 28th Division, where they state it's their policy to do this kind of thing, to tie down the VRS from going to the Sarajevo front. I don't know how many times I've argued that, since the Krstic case and the Blagojevic case, and now, again, I don't think we need to waste time, especially in 1994. Perhaps, as we get closer to our events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to comment, Mr. Petrusic? Mr. McCloskey, I understand your objection, of course, but it seems to me if you look at page 31 -- 41, sorry, lines 1 through 3, which refer to the basic question that Mr. Petrusic put to the witness, it's not exactly -- it doesn't exactly refer to what the armed forces of the Muslims did during 1994 or the period that he's referring the witness to, but, rather, what was the reaction of the Serb forces. But, again, we are not far off from the events that you mentioned and which, very rightly, put -- are not in contestation. Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Why don't you go straight to what is relevant to this case and which is contested by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to be able to reply in full to your question, or, rather, to respond to the objection raised by the Prosecution, perhaps it would be good for the witness to leave the courtroom. Or perhaps I might consult lead counsel, Ms. Fauveau, who might perhaps respond in French. It's not a problem. I'm -- I can do it, but it's a linguistic problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can quite understand. Perhaps you can consult with Madam Fauveau, first, and see whether you want to proceed with this matter or whether you want to move on to -- with your questions. Switch off your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Do you wish the witness to leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, if you could kindly leave the courtroom for a short while. We'll be calling you back soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I've been trying to show, or, rather, what the Defence has been trying to show by producing these documents are not facts, not the fact that attacks were launched from the enclaves or that there was a corridor linking the two enclaves. Enough documents have already been produced to prove those facts, and I am sure that the Trial Chamber will take them into account when deciding on these matters. These documents from the Drina Corps, from the army of Republika Srpska, are produced in order to show that even before Directive Number 7 was issued, there were problems there and that the army of Republika Srpska had been trying unsuccessfully to solve the military problem of the enclaves, to shut them up or dissolve them even before Directive Number 7 was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that in contestation, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, I think we have been giving you maps and battle plans from 1993 of the same thing. I think we started with the six strategic objectives. They have been trying to clear that area out for a long time, and that's not in contest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, I feel very uncomfortable in stopping you, Mr. Petrusic. On the other hand, you know, I mean, we can't go on with each and every witness that comes here from the VRS or from the previous JNA repeating the same story all over again when, for the past two and a half years, we have heard it for the umpteenth time and there is no disagreement on what happened both on the Muslim side and on the Serbian -- Bosnian Serbian side. Anyway, I don't know if you want to consult further with Madam Fauveau. I think we sent the message loud and clear. It's more interesting for us to proceed and hear the substance of the testimony of this gentleman, who, after all, is also being summoned by the Popovic and the Pandurevic Defence teams. Shall we bring the witness back?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Mr. President, very briefly just two sentences. The reason why we try to tender these documents and to examine the witness about those circumstances is to introduce the subjective element of the crime that is mentioned in the indictment, by providing this context, the Defence is trying to challenge the Prosecution allegation that after the Directive Number 9, or, rather, Directive Number 7 was issued, all those who were involved in the activities that related to Srebrenica was -- were aware of the criminal intent and thereby tried to -- or were involved in the criminal activity. It is our argument that the intent of the army of Republika Srpska was the same even before Directive Number 7 was issued and remained the same after its issuing. In other words, its conduct was legitimate. So there was no intent to cleanse the population from Srebrenica but to find a military solution for the problem of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Given that that was the position, why don't you go straight to 1995, Directive Number 7, and ask the witness whether anything changed with Directive Number 7. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, and I absolutely agree with Counsel in a way. We have targeted this indictment to begin in March with Directive 7, but I do believe that the same conduct was going on since the beginning of the war. We have not charged it here because we want this case to end eventually, and his -- he's got a different take on 1992 and 1993 and 1994, and that's fine, and we can argue about that, but we agree on everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Hope springs eternal. Let's continue. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will try not to object to that, but this is bringing me back to General Krstic, Mr. Petrusic and this witness, but I will try to refrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic, for your patience. Mr. Petrusic, bearing in mind what we have stated, I suggest you go straight to the point and avoid reviewing the historical background. And, of course, you are then free to ask whatever question you like, provided it's relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know that the forces of the Drina Corps were in contact with the forces from Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Drina Corps forces had sniper weapons in its armory?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I often toured the various front lines in the Drina Corps area of responsibility, and believe me when I say that I never saw a single soldier who was issued with a sniper rifle. I like weapons and that's why I know. Semi-automatic sniper rifles have only ten bullets, you can only fire single shots, and you can talk to any soldier and ask them, and they will all tell you that they preferred to have automatic weapons issued to them. And we didn't have such rifles at all in our stocks -- well, there were situations where shots were fired from light machine guns or semi-automatic rifles, and then when it buzzes past somebody's head, that person assumes that he was being targeted by a sniper. I know that such assumptions were made on our side, and probably it was done on the other side, too. So when single shots were fired, people assumed that those were snipers targeting them. But that's just that, assumptions, guesswork. I never saw any of our soldiers in positions around the enclaves or anywhere else -- I never say anyone carry sniper rifles when attacks were being launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could the witness be instructed to answer the question. That was at a simple question, "Do they have sniper rifles?" And he went on and on. If that goes on, we will be here forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know any dominant features around the protected area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with the features on -- to the east and to the south, Kuarac, Pribicevac, Javor, Teocak, Klokoc, Caurka, Bracan, Rogac, Ravni Buljin, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony you told us something about the road, Zeleni Jadar, the Zeleni Jadar road. Now I would like us to focus on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could I please have 5D1046.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the preamble of this document below the word "reference" and then could you please look at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version that's at page 2 and in the Serbian version you just need to scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have not had an opportunity to look at this order before, but now that I have read it I know about the situation, the situation that this order deals with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what situation are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here the Drina Corps, the command of the Drina Corps, orders some of the units that are deployed in that part of the Srebrenica enclave to take the features, geographic features, that remained -- or, rather, that couldn't have been taken before because of shortage of personnel. This is the area between the Skelani Battalion and the Milici Brigade positions. I am familiar with this area. About 7 kilometres were not covered, and we believed that this area was used by armed groups to move from one enclave to the other. So these are Kostur, Caurka, and Klokoc, those three features. In fact, I took part in this combat action -- or, rather, this was not a combat action, because not a single bullet was fired. I remembered when I read item number 5, it says that the signals chief will set up the communications in time to -- for the purpose of this task, and I was actually tasked with setting up the communications. I was at Pribicevac at the time, and I know that there was a heavy snowfall in the area. And attempts were made to reach those features. Since defence positions had not been set up there, I am talking about dugouts or bunkers, all the units after the march and the reconnaissance of those features, simply returned to their original units or commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of January, 1995, then was it difficult to access the village of Zeleni Jadar? Were there any problems there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember this quite well, when this operation ended in 1993 and when the UN forces entered Srebrenica, I, myself, went back to the command in Vlasenica using that road leading up to Zeleni Jadar, Jaseziovo, Podravanije, Milici, because it was under our control at the time, in the territory that we controlled. And later on when the borders of the demilitarised zone were set up, and I can't tell you now. I don't know exactly how this border went. I know that our units, in that area, because of the difficult terrain, pulled back and set up their defences to more favourable positions in other geographic features away from that road so that this road, at the beginning, was absolutely in our territory outside of the borders of the demilitarised zone. And I know that there were some problems later in that segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1227.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, this is a document from your command dated the 18th of March, 1995. Could you please look at the preamble. Could you please read it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this situation from March 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether anything was done at the time to liberate that road?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing was done at that time to liberate that road or, rather, to put it under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. The village itself of Zeleni Jadar is near the -- well, there is a cross-roads there, and there are only two or three factories there.
