And as I've already stated, after our defence positions were moved to more favourable places, that place remained more or less a no man's land, although it was technically on our side of the demarcation line. And this document shows that the other warring side, making use of the vicinity of various points where -- from where they could cover the valley with firepower, dismantled the industrial facilities, the plants that had remained there until March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And was the road still cut off, the one that was supposed to be liberated at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that in this period the units of the Drina Corps, which had organised defence in that area, were still not able to make a full use of that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware whether UNPROFOR took any -- undertook any activities to prevent the Muslim units and to protect the property in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I know that the UNPROFOR checkpoints was between Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica, but I am not aware of any activities to prevent the looting of property from those factories that is described in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D1082. 5D1082.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is a report from your command of the 23rd of May, 1995 [as interpreted]. Please look at point 2 and comment on it and on the events described here.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of the activities described in item 2 of this regular combat report of the command of the Drina Corps. The commander of the Drina Corps, with some of the officers from the command, was in the area of Zeleni Jadar, and he was in charge of the action as it says here, in the Zeleni Jadar valley. The result of that action was that the industrial plants were put under our control as was the Skelani-Jadar-Jasenova asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction in the transcript, please, page 50, line 21. Instead of the "23rd of May," it should say the "31st of May."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, who was in command of that action in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The direct commander was the corps commander, General Zivanovic. He had a team consisting of several officers from the corps, and I was in the area at the time in charge of organising signals or communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And where did you set up the communications line?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Pribicevac location, and I established communications with the small combat groups which had specific tasks in the Zeleni Jadar valley and along the Zeleni Jadar-Jasenova road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 52894, P2894.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order which the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, from the forward command post at Pribicevac, sent to the units participating in these activities around Zeleni Jadar, concerning physical control of these facilities and the asphalt road that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could we have page 2 of that document. Could we scroll down a little -- up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you read to us the handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It says here, "For the Skelani Battalion," or "The independent battalion Skelani. Jevdze [phoen] will convey this." It probably refers to me. Probably the order, signed by General Zivanovic, and we see his signature here, "as we didn't have a typewriter at the forward command post at the time this is probably typed out by the signalsman on the teleprinter, and he made copies for the units to which the order refers." I don't recall exactly, but probably whoever wrote this thought that I should take this order to the Skelani Battalion, which was on the left bank of the Zeleni Jadar river. They had their positions there, or something like that. I don't really remember what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It says, "In the second line, engage self-propelled guns at 0500 hours." Did you have self-propelled guns at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that we had self-propelled artillery weapons in that area and that they were used in the area for that particular task, but, well, they have a longer range, so perhaps whoever was planning this, I really don't know what this was about, thought they could be used from another location. But that command group included Colonel Veletic, and I think he was an artillery man, and he would probably know what this is about. I know that in that area at that time we didn't have these self-propelled weapons; although, as I say, their range is very long, and if somebody was planning this, they may have planned using them from a longer distance, but I can't really be precise about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This may be a translation issue, but I don't think so, but among the English version, I have I believe it's a receipt stamped of the Bratunac Brigade, not the IKM at Pribicevac, as the witness is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Could you address this to the witness himself who has heard Mr. McCloskey, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, are you speaking of the Pribicevac forward command post or the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Pribicevac forward command post, which was established by the Drina Corps command, for the needs of this activity in Zeleni Jadar. That's what I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, please, go back to the order. You have had occasion to see it, and tell me, please, did you about on it and if so how?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I had occasion to see this order recently a few days ago when preparing for this testimony. It does not refer specifically to me but to two smaller units which had a smaller number of men at the time and certain possibilities were incorporated in the plan that they might run into in the course of carrying out the task. I felt that this order was written using terminology which is not characteristic of highly trained officers, but, well, that's up to the person who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the end of this order, now that we are discussing it, please tell us when this action was carried out, was military force used?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I remember very vividly from that period is that I observed this activity with a great deal of apprehension, and the units to which this order refers took new positions; thus, leaving the asphalt road behind their backs without firing a single bullet which shows that this area was, in fact, no man's land at the time and that it was actually behind the demarcation line separating the two enclaves or, rather, separating the two warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that an UNPROFOR checkpoint was moved, was relocated at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that at that time an UNPROFOR checkpoint was relocated. It was moved closer to Zeleni Jadar along this asphalt road, running from Zeleni Jadar toward Srebrenica. But as I was at Pribicevac, and this area is in a valley, in a canyon, in fact, in a depression, I don't have any precise information as to how this was done and what the area in fact is, what size it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D1083.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report from the command of Drina Corps at Pribicevac dated the 13th of June, 1995 [as interpreted]. And in item 2, it says: "After the withdrawal of UNPROFOR, the inhabitants of Zeleni Jadar moved out in panic..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In fact it's paragraph 2 of item 1, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, bearing in mind this report, where it says that the population moved out, did the population really move out?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the area of Zeleni Jadar was a purely industrial zone with two or three factories. There was a factory producing furniture and another one producing marble. I didn't observe any residential houses in the area. And as a soldier I can draw the conclusion that even when the front end of our defence was moved to new facilities, leaving the road behind our backs, the units engaged in this did not come across any defensive positions of the enemy side, which is quite logical. And speaking from experience, I know that the population on both sides never lived and worked in front of the defensive positions of the army, but rather behind them so that it would not be logical to think that there was any civilian population living in Zeleni Jadar, because that would mean that they were living literally in front of the trenches and in front of the barrels of their own soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We needed a foundational question that he could see that from there, because the previous question, he said he's up in Pribicevac and he can't see the area of Zeleni Jadar. And then he starts describing all these things that aren't happening. So foundationally, we need to get to A before we get to B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I get you, Mr. McCloskey. Perhaps you could ask a direct question to the witness to explain -- asking him to explain how come he's giving this description.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, are you aware whether in that area there was any civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have already said, in that period in 1993, I passed through the cross-roads in Zeleni Jadar more than once, and I know that there were mostly industrial plants there and that there were no residential houses there, and the second part of my reply, why I think there were no people living there, is that the defensive positions of the 28th Divisions were downstream from Zeleni Jadar towards Srebrenica, and even if there was a residential house there, it would not be logical for people to live in front of the defence lines of their open army. The people always lived behind the backs of their own armies in every war theater I have ever been in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 54, line 15, instead of the date the "13th of June, 1995," it should say "the 3rd of June, 1995." Could we have page 2 of this report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, please look at the last sentence before item 3. Are you aware that the things mentioned in this report were captured?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you observe any modern premises as described here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: All the observations --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Foundational, the last one we saw was purely speculation and so if he's there and can see it, fine; but otherwise, this is speculative, like the last one was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Petrusic, I think Mr. McCloskey is right. He's -- you first have to ascertain with the witness what he could and couldn't see, or establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, when passing along this road, did you observe these modern specially built premises?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: On my return from this task, I was not relatively close to that checkpoint, but those were containers, all those observation posts were really prefabricated containers, if that can be described as a modern specially built premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In point 3 of this report, it says "We have had no casualties, we have expended small amounts of ammunition, and three zoljas," or handheld rocket launchers. Do you know whether these three zoljas were fired, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, I will withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Jevdjevic, if you could answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I had no information, nor did I know, that zoljas were used in this activity. I simply didn't hear about it, although Pribicevac is some 10 kilometres or less from Zeleni Jadar. But the detonation from a zolja would probably be heard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of the report, it says, "Major Milenko Jevdjevic." Did you compile this report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. To the best of my recollection, no. Because I was part of a time lead personally by the corps commander, and there were some highly positioned officers from the corps command there, and it seems almost incredible that I, as the most junior officer in rank, in charge of organising signals, would be given the task of compiling this lengthy report in which there is information which I have seen now first time. And anyway, it was not my duty at the time, while I was engaged in communications, to draw up reports for these commands. And, finally, I do not see my signature here, although a telegram can be sent in such a way that the signature is not visible. However, I do not remember compiling a report like this when the corps commander and his other officers were there at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as to how it's possible that your name appears on this report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply it sounds very illogical. When the corps commander is personally in charge of an action, to send a report to the staff commander, that would be a superior sending a report to a junior officer. And furthermore, I see that this report arrived in the corps command at around 2120 hours, that it was deciphered at 2125, and I think that on the 3rd, I was probably not in the area anymore, that I had already left and arrived in the corps command before this report. I assume that one of those officers did that who were there, but why my name is mentioned here, I really would not want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there is a -- maybe a translation error in the English. It says "The GS VRS to the Chief of Staff personally" in what I've got, and I look at the -- what I think is the one you are talking about, and it says "Command of the Drina Corps." I might be wrong, but it sounds -- it looks like a pretty significant translation issue, or I've mixed up the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you there. Yes, but perhaps, Mr. Petrusic, you are in a better position than we are to deal with this. But I think from what I see here -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, obviously there is a mistake in the transcript. So you were talking about who -- whom this report was sent to, here it says "to the Main Staff of the VRS." Could you please look at this report and tell us whom it was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: If the usher could please take us back to the beginning of the document. This report was sent from the forward command post of the Drina Corps at Pribicevac, which was under the direct command of the Drina Corps command, it was sent to the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps command at the Drina Corps command. That's what it says here. In military terms, it is quite illogical for the corps commander, who is present at a place, in charge of an activity personally, to be sending a report from that location to his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, are you familiar with any other activities that the Drina Corps in the spring of 1995 was engaged in in its area of responsibility in concerted action with the East Bosnian Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am best familiar with an action that the Drina Corps engaged in in the broader area from Zvornik to Majevica. In response to a large-scale offensive mounted by the enemy that had preceded it, and this is when the Drina Corps in concerted action with the forces of the East Bosnia Corps, carried out an operation in the broader area between Zvornik and Majevica; to be more specific, in the direction of Teocuk. That was the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what was the code name of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: That operation had the code name Spreca, Spreca 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not the exact time that we usually take our break, but I would like to explore this topic at some length and perhaps this would be a good time for a break in that light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not fight with you for two minutes, Mr. Petrusic. Let's have the break now, 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you told us that you knew about Operation Spreca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 5D975 up on the screen. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, could you please look at this order and could you please tell us whether you have any knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I actually do have some knowledge about implementation of what this order discusses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the 4th Serb Light Infantry Brigade was actually established?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection it was established sometime in late March or early April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you in any way participate in that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a task force, and I was assigned to be the Chief of Staff of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what task did this brigade have?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly to the best of my recollection, that brigade was tasked to operate in concerted action with other units of the Drina Corps to stabilize this front line in the broader Majevica region, and to carry out attacks in concerted action with the East Bosnian Corps, in an effort to cut off this pocket in the Majevica area, Teocuk, Sapna, and some other smaller villages were located there in that pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you then stop performing your regular duties in line with this order? In other words, we are talking about establishing communications and maintaining communications.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, while I was temporarily engaged in this task force, in that period of time, I was not the commander of the signals battalion and I can only assume that probably I was replaced by one of my officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D983 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to this document, could you please tell us me where your command post or your forward command post was during the Operation Spreca?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was located in a village north of Zvornik. I think it's Trsic, it was called Trsic, it was in the school building, the elementary school of that village. I am referring to the command post of the 4th Serb Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This document, 5D983, bears this code name Spreca 95. It's a combat order, and now I would like us to look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the penultimate page until the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you can see here just before item 3, it says: "IKM of the GS VRS in Zvornik." Did you know that a forward command post of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska was established in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As you went about your business as the Chief of Staff of this unit, the 4th Serb Brigade, did you have any contacts with the officers at the forward command post, the IKM, of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: We, in the 4th Serb Brigade, did not have any direct contact with the officers from the forward command post of the Main Staff in Zvornik, because the Drina Corps itself had set up its own forward command post in Zvornik in the Zvornik Brigade command. And I know that the corps commander himself was there quite often, so it was quite logical that we were more often in contact with the corps command and with its forward command post in Zvornik, and I assume that it was in turn in contact with the forward command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know which of the officers from the Main Staff actually was at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any specific knowledge because the brigade commander, Colonel Veletic, attended the briefings in most cases. I think that I went there only once because some military tasks were given out. I think that there were a few officers there. They were rotating from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did any name stick in your mind? I am not insisting now if you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I may have seen General Milovanovic as I passed by. I don't know whether he was heading in the direction of the East Bosnia Corps at that time. And I assume that some of the officers from the logistics organ in the Main Staff were there, or some of the operations officers, because those were the key functions for -- the key posts for the functioning of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you have any operation officers at your forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Serb Brigade did have its operations officer, if that's what you're referring to. The operations officer, who was again taken from one of the subordinate units and assigned to that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Jevdjevic, please, if you could be kind enough to allow a short interval before you start giving your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, the role of your operations officer, was it important?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, his role was important for the functioning of the staff segment of the command of the 4th Serb Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you said that even at the forward command post of the Main Staff at Zvornik, there were some operations officers, but please ... yes, do go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that it was the case. That was the logic, that's how it worked. I can't really recall the officers who were actually there, but it is usually -- it is usual military practice. Logistics officers are always important. From our point of view -- so somebody from the logistics organ, from the Main Staff, had to be there in order to organise the supply of the units that participated in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know that in July 1995 there was an operation in the Drina Corps area, its code name was Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what does this operation mean and when did it begin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before the operation began, I knew that the units of the Drina Corps were tasked --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, we'll get to that. I do apologise for interrupting you, but what I am interested in is for you to tell us what did this code name mean in translation, Krivaja 95, and when the operation was actually launched.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Krivaja 95 is just a name, like any other name that is assigned to an operation. Krivaja is just a river in Bosnia, and probably those who planned the operation gave it this name. And the operation itself started in early July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at document 5DP106. The document is 5DP106. Could we please look at page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a preparatory order issued by the command of the Drina Corps which it issued on the 2nd of July 1995 to its subordinated units with the task of carrying out preparations for the forthcoming operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To whom was this document sent, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This document was sent, as it says here, to the commands of the Zvornik Brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade, the 1st and 5th Podrinje Brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment of the Drina Corps, and the Skelani Independent Infantry Battalion; in other words, to the subordinate units of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 2 and tell us whether this is the task given to the subordinate units in this preparatory order.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this lists all the tasks issued to the subordinate units by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of Directive 7 and Directive 7/1?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In this task, is there any separation of Srebrenica and Zepa and any narrowing down to the city area, the town area, in these items 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not there in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P107 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, this is a document issued by the same command as the previous document, and it bears the title "Command of" -- or "Order for Active Combat Activities Operation Number 1." Can you tell us to which order this unit was issued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I hate to interrupt you, but do we have to go through this? Can't we see it ourselves. If there is a problem with anybody who may have or may not have received this document, I can understand the question, To whom was it sent, but otherwise, I can read it, I don't need the witness to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, in relation to the previous document, the document you have before you, was it sent to all the units?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This particular document was not sent to all the units to which the preparatory order of the same date was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page of this document, please. Actually, in English it's the page before last.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the nature of this document, do you know who participated in its drawing up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The entire corps command participated in compiling this order, everyone dealing with the aspect that he was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In item 11, we have command and communications. Did you participate in compiling this document as far as this item goes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any informations as to whether anyone from communications participated in drawing up this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When this document is concerned, and every other document where communications are planned, it was the chief of communications of the corps who had exclusive competence and power to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what was your relation to the chief of communications of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to subordination within the corps? The chief of communications was an advisory organ advising the Chief of Staff, and professionally he was superior to the communications Battalion; that is, to me, but only as far as the professional side of our work was concerned. As for the military and disciplinary aspects, we were subordinate directly to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to page 2 of this document in the Serbian version; whereas it's page 3 in the English version, item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, in line 3 of item 4, it says: "The more immediate task is to reach the ..." and so on. What does that mean, "the more immediate task"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The more immediate task was given to the units as a line on the ground which the units are supposed to reach in the first offensive action, the first assault, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Two lines further down, it says "The next task ..." and so on and so forth. My question is, when is the next task carried out, is there a deadline, is there a timeline, is it implied automatically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do we have just one foundational question? I mean, he says he didn't take part in the making of this, he doesn't know about the things that are cited in it, was he given this, did he study it, was he part of the operation? That one question would tell us; otherwise, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you handle this or would you handle this, Mr. Petrusic, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, were you a participant of the Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of Banja Guber, Zivko, Brdo, Divjakenje [phoen], Gradac, and so on, as parts of military terminology?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You explained the what the immediate task of the next task means, or, rather, what the immediate task means, and now my question is what does the next task imply?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The next task is the task which the units carry out after they have carried out the immediate task pursuant to orders and approval from the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does this imply that the next task is obligatory, that it must be ordered?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's already regulated in the order itself. On the ground, in practical terms, it depends on the decision of the commander in charge of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see now document P3753 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you see this document. Tell us, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It seems to consist of several parts. Can you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The first part is a work plan for the radio network used for command in the Operation Krivaja 95. And the second part, underneath it, with the small dense writing, is a signals table. These are the usual military terms adapted for this purpose in case some orders need to be encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So this signals table means that these numbers are written instead of the words we see here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To transmit certain information or convey a certain order, when you have a message, one could use a combination of certain numbers in order to convey to another unit certain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to the first part where we have several participants -- or, rather, more participants than are mentioned in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If you remember, there were six participants in the order, so I'm interested on what basis did the chief of communications or whoever drew up this document include more participants in the communications plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Whenever such work plans are drawn up for radio networks, the possibility is always envisaged that some of the participants in the radio communication, that is, some of the units, who are within the radio network used for commanding the operation, should also include at least two reserve units in case new possibilities open up. This has to be flexible to avoid having to draw up a new plan simply because another unit has been added on or resubordinated or attached. So this is done in order to be able to deal with new situations. That's why at least two reserve participants are always included.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: These frequency ranges, the ones in megahertz, can you tell us on what sort of equipment these frequencies may be used?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a work plan for a radio network which we had with a radio apparatus called RUP-2/2K, which is similar and compatible to RUP-12 as regards the frequencies and number of channels. A good side of this equipment was that it was modified in such a way that crypto -- crypto-protection could be attached to it, a special device could be attached to it, and it worked on 32, 79.89 megahertz or hertz, and the frequencies mentioned here 1 to 20, this is not a frequency but the position of three switches used to take up a certain frequency. In our signals terminology this referred to a channel, for example, channel 250 doesn't mean that the frequency is 250 megahertz, because I have already told you what the frequency range is. But one can easily calculate what the frequency would be. It doesn't really matter right now, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us this last column here, letters and numbers, what is this all about? And below this, we can read that it says "Table Tesla."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an instruction so that if this radio network experiences some problems, such as, for instance, if it is being disrupted or jammed by other participants or by the enemy, or if this was going on at a certain time of day or night when electro-magnetic waves move in a particular way, then this made it possible to change the work channel if this channel no longer meets the requirements. And here it is indicated that the working channel should be switched. This is confidential and this is in code. Well, I can't really read it, because it's not very legible, but let's say for instance you have a word here, and then it says "15," and this means that all the participants should switch to channel 15, which is envisaged here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you receive this document when you set off for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, could you please tell us when did you set off to Srebrenica and who issued you that -- you the direct order, the marching orders in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I set off on the 5th of July, that was when I started implementing this operation, and I assume that I received those documents from the chief of communications or signals. Since I can't recall having received it from the corps commander or the Chief of Staff, and it was quite usual for the communications chief once the communications plan is drafted in accordance with the orders of the corps commander, to deliver this communications plan to the unit that is supposed to implement it in accordance with the professional line of command. So I assume that he issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you recall who ordered you to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was either the corps commander or the Chief of Staff, well, one of the two. I can't recall. But it was just a task for me. Perhaps it was even the communications chief who relayed this to me, but I can't really recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As far as the equipment is concerned, the communications equipment, can you tell us what you had? What kind of equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: For the implementation of this task, I had at my disposal radio equipment with speech encryption technology, and I used them to set up communications with the subordinate units participating in Operation Krivaja 95. As for the communications with the superior command, the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica, I used the radio relay equipment RRU1, and this made it possible for us to send written reports that were first encrypted. And my encryption officer who went with me had appropriate encryption equipment. Again, he also had the teleprinters in order to be able to send those encrypted telegrams. So this was the equipment that I had with me in order to implement this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did the Main Staff or the 67th Signals Regiment or the chief of the Main Staff, did they provide you with any elements necessary to establish your communications at the forward command post of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. This was an operation of the Drina Corps. It used only its own forces, and there was no need to involve the Main Staff or the signals regiment of the Main Staff for the implementation of this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1105.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll down a little so that we can see the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It was issued in the morning of the 5th of July, 1995. Could you please tell us when did you actually head for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I started on the 5th of July. I would say it was around 10 or 1100 hours; in the morning, at any rate. And I arrived at the forward command post at Pribicevac in the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before you set off to set up the communications centre at the forward command post at Pribicevac, did you know what tasks were issued to the Drina Corps units participating in this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew roughly what these were, because I did not receive the order with the tasks, but I did know roughly -- or, rather, I knew specifically what units were participating and what more or less were their key tasks on those axes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you, Mr. Petrusic, we stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, did you know the equivalent of the forces in numerical terms that participated in the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I did know that there on the spot, so to speak. I knew what units participated and I knew, more or less, their equivalent on the ground. And all those units that were from the broader region, from the south, attacking -- or, rather, carrying out this task, they, all told, did not go beyond the strength of 1.000 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Now, if we compare it to 1993, let us draw this parallel, this is when you again participated in that area, that was before the protected areas were set up, can you tell us whether this time the forces were stronger or weaker, numerically speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vague. I don't understand what operation is he talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we leave it until tomorrow? Okay. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow in the afternoon, like today, 2.15. Thank you.
